hints: Look closely at the wall of the vessel in the micrograph and the dark red blood cells inside. How thick is the wall, and how many red cells can fit side by side in the lumen?
Remember that only one type of vessel has a wall made of endothelium only, with no muscle or elastic layers, and a lumen just wide enough for red cells to pass in single file.
walkthrough:
**Observe the clues in the micrograph**

Look at the vessel labelled. The wall is extremely thin, just a single dark line of cells. Inside, the dark red blood cells are squeezed through in a single file line, almost touching the wall.

There is no thick muscle, elastic or collagen layer visible.

**Recall the structure of each vessel type**

Arterioles have endothelium plus a layer of smooth muscle to control vasoconstriction. Venules and veins have endothelium plus some connective tissue and muscle, and a wider lumen.

Capillaries are different. Their wall is endothelium only, one cell thick, to allow rapid exchange. Their lumen is about $7-8 \mu m$ wide, just enough for one red blood cell at a time.

**Match the evidence to the vessel**

Thin one-cell wall plus very narrow lumen plus single file red cells matches a capillary perfectly. It is too thin and too narrow to be an arteriole, venule or vein.

options.A: Arteriole is false because arterioles have smooth muscle in the wall for vasoconstriction, which is not seen here.
options.B: Capillary is correct because the wall is endothelium only and the lumen holds red blood cells in single file for exchange.
options.C: Vein is false because veins are much larger with thicker walls containing connective tissue and muscle, and a wide lumen.
options.D: Venule is false because venules are wider than capillaries and have more than just endothelium in their wall.
